strengths: Provides a rigorous information-theoretic analysis of weight-only linear layer quantization, showing that GPTQ/Huffman-GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large rate gap to the high-rate waterfilling limit.

Introduces a novel and elegant algorithm, WaterSIC, that implements unequal per-column quantization rates via a Cholesky/SIC formulation and is proven to be within 0.255 bits of the information-theoretic limit in the high-rate asymptotic regime.

The connection between GPTQ and successive interference cancellation/Babai's algorithm is cleanly developed, and the waterfilling interpretation motivates a simple, theoretically grounded modification.

Strong empirical results: WaterSIC establishes new state-of-the-art WikiText-2 perplexity across 1–4 bit rates on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-2-7B, often with substantial margins over Huffman-GPTQ, QTIP, NestQuant, and AWQ.

Includes extensive appendices with algorithmic details, ablations, entropy-coding verification, KL-divergence comparisons, and zero-shot accuracy evaluations, supporting the practical effectiveness of the method.

The limitations section honestly acknowledges the absence of end-to-end throughput benchmarking, large-scale model evaluation, and integration with fine-tuning, which helps contextualize the contribution.
weaknesses: The theoretical near-optimality guarantee is asymptotic (large number of rows, high-rate/low-distortion limit) and assumes i.i.d. Gaussian weights; the full practical WaterSIC algorithm, with its many heuristics, is not covered by the proof, so the 0.255-bit claim does not directly extend to the deployed method.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a code release and by several model-specific or data-dependent hyperparameter choices (adaptive mixing coefficients, damping, dead-feature threshold, manual removal of outlier rows in Qwen3-8B), which may make exact replication difficult.

Evaluation is restricted to small and mid-sized models (up to 8B parameters); no results are provided for larger LLMs, and there is no measurement of actual compression/decompression throughput or interaction with hardware kernels, despite entropy coding being central to the method.

Some baseline comparisons use different rate-reporting conventions (entropy vs. log-cardinality) and several baseline numbers are taken from prior work rather than reproduced under identical calibration conditions, which could affect the fairness of the comparisons.

The claim that all existing algorithms fix the same quantization rate for all columns is too strong: some mixed-precision PTQ methods already allocate different rates or bitwidths across channels/groups, even if not in the exact waterfilling form.

The practical algorithm modifies the model via dead-feature erasure and outlier-row zeroing, which may introduce calibration-set-specific effects; generalization to other datasets, domains, or model families is not fully established.
The computational cost of the per-layer binary searches and golden-section searches for adaptive mixing is not reported, and it may be substantial for large models or large calibration sets.

strengths: Introduces a simple and well-motivated per-column rate allocation scheme (alpha_i = c / l_ii) for GPTQ/SIC, connecting GPTQ to lattice decoding and waterfilling.
Provides an asymptotic high-rate analysis showing that the proposed PlainWaterSIC is within 0.255 bits of the waterfilling lower bound, while standard GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap.

Reports substantial empirical improvements over entropy-coded GPTQ (Huffman-GPTQ) and other baselines on Llama and Qwen family models, with detailed ablations, zero-shot evaluations, and diagnostic plots.
Includes a relatively honest limitations section and extensive appendices documenting hyperparameters and implementation details.
weaknesses: Unfair rate comparison: WaterSIC reports entropy-coded rates while several baselines (AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTQ, RTN) report log-cardinality. This inflates the claimed SOTA results; a fair comparison would entropy-code all methods or report WaterSIC's nominal code length.

The central theoretical claim applies only to the asymptotic high-rate iid Gaussian setting and to PlainWaterSIC, not to the full WaterSIC pipeline, which includes many unanalyzed heuristics (LMMSE correction, diagonal rescalers, activation drift/residual correction, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure).

No empirical validation of the 0.255-bit gap is provided for practical 1–4 bit rates. The high-rate assumptions underlying the theorem fail in this regime, so the paper's claims of near-optimality and 'SOTA for all quantization rates' are not supported at the rates actually evaluated.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete or potentially inconsistent: Qwen3-8B baselines are taken from Chen et al. (2025) under a possibly different evaluation/calibration setup; Table 2 has missing entries at 2.625 and 3.625 bits; and dead-feature erasure is applied to WaterSIC but apparently not to GPTQ, which may advantage WaterSIC.
The claim that all existing algorithms fix the same quantization rate for all columns is inaccurate; many PTQ methods use per-channel scaling, mixed precision, or group-wise rates.

Practical significance and reproducibility are limited: entropy coding/Huffman is not hardware-friendly, no throughput/latency or end-to-end compression speed is measured, no code is released, and stochastic elements (10% row sampling, per-layer golden search) are not accompanied by variance or seed analysis.
The Qwen3-8B preprocessing step that zeros outlier rows and verifies the change on WikiText-2 test perplexity may constitute test-set usage for model selection.
Presentation is dense and notationally inconsistent across algorithms (e.g., L, A, alpha, c), and some figures omit baselines or use visually misleading large-PPL cutoffs.

strengths: The paper provides a novel information-theoretic analysis of GPTQ for linear-layer quantization, showing that canonical GPTQ is equivalent to ZSIC with a fixed spacing matrix A = αI and can have an arbitrarily large gap to the waterfilling lower bound (Eq. 13).

It proposes WaterSIC, which allocates different quantization rates to different input features via α_i = c/|l_ii|, and proves an asymptotic rate gap of at most 0.255 bits to the IT limit for iid Gaussian weight rows (Theorem 3.3). This is a clean and meaningful theoretical contribution.

The practical algorithm includes several well-motivated components (LMMSE correction, activation drift correction, residual-stream correction, diagonal rescalers, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure) with detailed ablations and diagnostics in the appendix.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: WaterSIC achieves state-of-the-art WikiText-2 perplexity on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-2-7B across roughly 1–4 bits, outperforming Huffman-GPTQ, GPTQ, RTN, QTIP, NestQuant, and AWQ in many settings (Tables 1–2, 7–8; Figures 1–3, 12–13).
Zero-shot accuracy evaluations on Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-8B show improvements over Huffman-GPTQ at matched rates (Tables 9–10).

The paper includes a clear limitations section and discusses ethical considerations; it also provides detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, calibration protocol, and lossless-codec checks in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
The work is original in combining waterfilling rate allocation with GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation, and the theory gives useful insight into why uniform-rate GPTQ is suboptimal.
weaknesses: The central near-optimality claim is asymptotic (a→∞, D→0) and assumes iid Gaussian weight rows. No synthetic Gaussian experiments or finite-rate analysis validate the 0.255-bit gap at practical 1–4 bit rates; the abstract's 'uniformly over all possible covariance matrices' omits the high-rate/asymptotic caveat.

Empirical gains are confounded: the full WaterSIC pipeline contains many additional calibration heuristics beyond unequal-rate waterfilling (Qronos, residual compensation, attention weighting, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure). The paper does not isolate the effect of per-column rates by comparing the full pipeline against the same pipeline with fixed per-column rates, so the SOTA improvements cannot be attributed solely to the claimed key innovation.

Baseline comparisons are uneven. For Qwen3-8B, Huffman-GPTQ/GPTQ/RTN numbers are taken from Chen et al. (2025) rather than rerun under the authors' protocol, and several strong baselines (e.g., AQLM, PV-Tuning, QuIP# on main models) are not compared. Some hyperparameters (e.g., damping δ for Llama-3-8B) appear tuned on WikiText-2 test perplexity rather than a held-out validation set.

The theoretical lower bound allows the decoder to depend on Σ_X, but the original problem does not. Achieving the waterfilling bound in the original setup may require sending the SVD basis, which costs O(1) bits per entry and could be non-negligible relative to the 0.255-bit gap. The paper acknowledges this but does not incorporate it into the analysis.

Presentation and notation issues: rate R is defined inconsistently (total bits vs. bits per entry), Algorithm 1 has duplicated lines, and Algorithms 3–4 contain index typos and notation errors (e.g., k vs. i, duplicated Σ entries), which hinder reimplementation.

No code release or end-to-end compression/decompression throughput benchmark is provided; hardware implications are left to future work. Evaluation is limited to relatively small/mid-sized models (1B, 7B, 8B), and scaling to larger models is not demonstrated.

strengths: Provides a rigorous information-theoretic framework for weight-only quantization of a linear layer under iid Gaussian weights, deriving the fundamental rate-distortion limit and showing that standard GPTQ/Huffman-GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to this limit.

Introduces a simple yet powerful theoretical insight: the optimal per-column quantization spacing should be proportional to the inverse Cholesky diagonal of the activation covariance, which implements waterfilling rate allocation without requiring an explicit rotation into the PCA basis.

Proves that PlainWaterSIC achieves a uniform rate gap of at most 0.255 bits to the IT limit for any positive semi-definite covariance matrix, with rigorous proofs in the appendix using lattice flatness factors and Rényi entropy.

Extensive experiments on multiple LLM families (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) across 1–4 bit rates demonstrate state-of-the-art perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, often with substantial margins over strong baselines.

The practical algorithm is well-motivated and includes several thoughtful improvements (LMMSE correction, activation drift and residual stream corrections, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, and post-quantization finetuning) with detailed hyperparameters, ablations, and diagnostics.

The paper includes a limitations section and extensive appendix analysis of calibration/finetuning dataset effects, Gaussianity checks, and actual codec compression rates, which aids reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (0.255-bit gap) applies to the idealized PlainWaterSIC under iid Gaussian weights and the high-rate/low-distortion limit. The full WaterSIC used in experiments contains many additional heuristics and per-layer hyperparameter tuning that are not covered by the formal bound, and the paper sometimes conflates the two.

The main empirical comparisons are not fully isolated: WaterSIC includes activation drift correction, residual stream compensation, attention weighting, and LMMSE/rescaler optimizations, while baselines such as Huffman-GPTQ use only quantized activation statistics. A direct ablation of equal versus unequal rate allocation within the same full pipeline would better support the claim that waterfilling is the primary driver of the gains.

Rate reporting is not uniform across methods: WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ report entropy-based rates, whereas many baselines use log-cardinality. Although the authors follow the conventions of the respective references, this complicates direct bitrate comparisons, and end-to-end (de)compression throughput and hardware feasibility are not benchmarked.

Reproducibility is somewhat challenging: the manuscript states 'Our code is available here' without a visible link, and the algorithm involves model-specific interventions (e.g., zeroing outlier rows in Qwen3-8B, dead-feature erasure) and per-layer golden-section search over mixing parameters. Optimizing per-layer hyperparameters on the calibration set may also risk overfitting to the calibration distribution.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with minor typos (e.g., 'ane', 'gquantization') and occasional equation inconsistencies. The Gaussianity assumption is only partially validated (q/k projections deviate), and the impact of this deviation on the theoretical guarantees is not quantified.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated idea: applying waterfilling/prediction-based rate allocation to linear-layer PTQ via unequal per-column quantization rates derived from the Cholesky diagonal.

Provides a useful information-theoretic perspective on GPTQ, showing that equal-spacing Huffman-GPTQ can be suboptimal and that WaterSIC attains a 0.255-bit gap to the waterfilling lower bound under high-rate Gaussian assumptions.

Empirical results across Llama/Qwen models and multiple bitrates show consistent improvements over several baselines, sometimes substantial (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B at 2 bits: WaterSIC 16.19 vs. Huffman-GPTQ 86.80 and QTIP 18.67).
The algorithm is described in substantial detail, with an appendix containing ablations and diagnostics for individual components.
The limitations section acknowledges the lack of hardware throughput benchmarking and the limited scale of models tested.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are asymptotic (D→0, a→∞) and assume iid Gaussian weight rows. The abstract and introduction overstate them as being uniform over all covariance matrices and as near-optimal at practical 1–4 bit rates; no finite-rate or non-Gaussian guarantees are provided.

The comparison to GPTQ is a strawman. Standard GPTQ implementations often use per-channel/group scales and are frequently combined with rotations (QuIP, QuaRot), which the paper ignores. The claim that 'all existing algorithms fix the same quantization rate for all columns' is false (e.g., AWQ, grouped GPTQ, mixed-precision methods).

Rate accounting is not apples-to-apples: WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ report rates via entropy, while several baselines report log-cardinality. This can make WaterSIC appear better than it is; actual compressed bitstreams should be used for all methods.

The state-of-the-art claim relies heavily on WaterSIC-FT, which fine-tunes on WikiText-2 train and is evaluated on WikiText-2 test. It sometimes surpasses BF16 PPL (e.g., Qwen3-8B at 4.125 bits: 9.67 vs. 9.73), while baselines are not similarly fine-tuned. This is an unfair comparison and suggests domain adaptation rather than pure quantization gains.

There is no clean ablation isolating the effect of unequal rate allocation from the many engineering tricks added in Section 4 (drift correction, residual-stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure). The improvement over Huffman-GPTQ therefore cannot be attributed to the central waterfilling innovation alone.

Test-set leakage: for Qwen3-8B, the authors use WikiText-2 test perplexity to justify zeroing specific outlier rows and then evaluate on the same WikiText-2 test set. This invalidates the reported Qwen3-8B results and raises methodological concerns.

Reproducibility is weak: the code link says only 'available here' with no URL; the pipeline involves many hyperparameters, per-layer golden-section searches, manual outlier removal, and no runtime/memory or seed/variance reporting.

Presentation issues are numerous: typos ('ane', 'trelises', 'Kroncker', 'calibratrion', 'gquantization'), inconsistent loss descriptions (KL vs. cross-entropy), references to 2026 papers, and several unclear algorithmic details.
The practical algorithm is complex, heuristically tuned, and not shown to scale to larger models; hardware/throughput evaluation is absent (acknowledged but still a limitation for a PTQ method).

The title and abstract claim 'Information-Theoretically Optimal' and 'near optimal' while the proven gap is only 0.255 bits for scalar quantization under high-rate asymptotics; the gap is not proven uniform over Σ_X or for finite distortion.

The practical motivation against PCA/waterfilling is weakened by fixed random rotations (e.g., Hadamard), which can be applied without sending an n×n SVD basis and are widely used in prior PTQ work; the paper does not compare against rotated GPTQ.

Several reported improvements are small and lack significance testing or error bars (e.g., 3.76 bits: WaterSIC 9.99 vs. NestQuant 10.06; 4.00 bits: 9.92 vs. 10.06), making it difficult to judge robustness.

strengths: Provides a novel information-theoretic framing for weight-only post-training quantization, connecting GPTQ-style successive quantization to lattice decoding and waterfilling rate allocation.

Derives a clean theoretical result: with an appropriate per-column spacing choice, WaterSIC achieves a rate gap of at most 0.255 bits to the waterfilling lower bound, uniformly over covariance matrices, while GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap.

The key algorithmic innovation—allocating different quantization rates to different input features based on the Cholesky diagonal (conditional variances)—is simple, well-motivated, and theoretically grounded.
Extensive empirical evaluation across Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3-70B, and Qwen3-8B, covering 1–4 bit rates, multiple benchmarks, and both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy.

The practical algorithm includes several well-ablated components (LMMSE correction, activation drift correction, residual stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing) that address real LLM quantization challenges.
Reproducibility is supported by released code, detailed appendices, hyperparameter tables, and an honest limitations section discussing layerwise MSE, hardware throughput, and model scale.
weaknesses: The theoretical near-optimality guarantee applies to PlainWaterSIC under idealized assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian weights, high-rate regime, layerwise Euclidean distortion), while the full WaterSIC used in experiments is a complex heuristic pipeline not covered by the theorem.

The claim that canonical GPTQ is equivalent to ZSIC with A = αI may not match standard GPTQ implementations that use per-column scales; the theoretical gap for GPTQ may therefore characterize a simplified variant rather than the practical baseline.

Several baseline comparisons rely on numbers taken from other papers (e.g., Qwen3-8B from Chen et al., Llama-3-70B from Huang et al.) with potentially different calibration/evaluation protocols, rather than re-evaluating all methods under the same controlled setting.

Rate reporting mixes entropy-coded bits (for WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ) with log-cardinality bits (for fixed-rate methods), which is not a perfectly apples-to-apples comparison despite following prior conventions.

The method is computationally and implementationally complex, involving per-layer golden-section search, secant rate matching, adaptive mixing, and manual model-specific interventions (e.g., zeroing outlier rows in Qwen3-8B), which may limit practical adoption and generalizability.

The 'new state-of-the-art for all rates from 1 to 4 bits' claim is slightly overstated: at 2 bits on Llama-2-7B, PV-Tuning reports competitive or better W2 perplexity, and 1-bit results are not compared against specialized 1-bit methods.
The paper does not benchmark end-to-end compression/decompression throughput, latency, or memory overhead, which are important for real deployment and are only briefly acknowledged as future work.
